questions.prompt: Explain why async code has to be 'async all the way down', and what goes wrong when a caller blocks on a task instead of awaiting it.

keyPoints.text: Awaiting makes asynchrony propagate to every caller up the chain.
keyPoints.quote: Once you `await`, the asynchrony flows up the call chain.

keyPoints.text: Even a console entry point can be async, so there is no need to block at the top.
keyPoints.quote: in a console app, `Main` can be `async Task`

keyPoints.text: Blocking with .Result or .Wait() is the rule you must never break.
keyPoints.quote: Never block on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.

keyPoints.text: The deadlock happens because the blocked thread is the one the continuation needs.
keyPoints.quote: the blocked thread is the very one the continuation needs to resume on, so nothing proceeds

keyPoints.text: Reading .Result is only safe on a task already known to be finished, e.g. right after WhenAll.
keyPoints.quote: The only place you might see `.Result` safely is on a task you *know* is already completed

keyPoints.text: async void is never written except for event handlers.

questions.prompt: Explain how to run independent async operations concurrently, and how exceptions behave when you do.

keyPoints.text: Awaiting one call after another serialises them.
keyPoints.quote: tasks one after another runs them

keyPoints.text: WhenAll is the tool for running independent I/O concurrently.
keyPoints.quote: `Task.WhenAll` is how you parallelize independent I/O.

keyPoints.text: WhenAny finishes with the first task, which suits timeouts and races.
keyPoints.quote: `Task.WhenAny` completes when the first task finishes (useful for timeouts/races).

keyPoints.text: Concurrent operations must be truly independent - not sharing one DbContext.
keyPoints.quote: `WhenAll` is for independent operations (separate HTTP calls, separate contexts).

keyPoints.text: An exception thrown inside an async method lives in the Task until it is awaited.
keyPoints.quote: Exceptions thrown in an async method are captured in the returned `Task` and re-thrown when you `await` it.

keyPoints.text: With several failures, await shows only the first; Task.Exception keeps all of them.
keyPoints.quote: if multiple tasks throw, `await` surfaces the first exception; the `Task.Exception` holds all of them as an `AggregateException`.

questions.prompt: Explain cancellation, ConfigureAwait(false) and Task.Run: when each belongs in your code and when it does not.

keyPoints.text: A CancellationToken is only useful if it is passed on to every async call.
keyPoints.quote: Honor it by passing it to every async call you make.

keyPoints.text: Cancellation shows up as an exception when the task is awaited.
keyPoints.quote: Cancellation surfaces as an `OperationCanceledException` / `TaskCanceledException` when awaited.

keyPoints.text: ConfigureAwait(false) is for reusable libraries, not app or controller code.
keyPoints.quote: add `ConfigureAwait(false)` in reusable libraries; don't bother in app/controller code.

keyPoints.text: ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, which is why it is unnecessary there.
keyPoints.quote: In ASP.NET Core app code it's unnecessary (there's no special synchronization context).

keyPoints.text: Wrapping I/O in Task.Run just burns a thread; use the native async API.
keyPoints.quote: But don't wrap I/O calls in `Task.Run` — that just wastes a thread.

keyPoints.text: In web apps Task.Run is rarely right; it mainly keeps desktop UIs responsive.
keyPoints.quote: In a web app, `Task.Run` is rarely the right tool; it's more for desktop apps keeping the UI responsive.
